DOCUMENT:
Policy Brief: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics
Riverside County Education Authority, Policy Unit, January 2026

Summary
In 2024-25 the Authority funded a pilot of high-dose mathematics tutoring for Year 7 pupils in six urban secondary schools. Pupils who received tutoring made substantially more progress than a randomly selected comparison group. This brief recommends extending the programme to all 42 secondary schools in the county from September 2026, at an estimated annual cost of £2.9 million.

The pilot
Tutoring was delivered in groups of three pupils, three one-hour sessions a week, for 30 weeks, during the school day. Tutors were undergraduate and postgraduate students from Riverside University, recruited, trained and paid £16 an hour through the University's Education Department. Pupils were eligible if they had scored below the expected standard in the end-of-primary mathematics assessment.

Of 480 eligible pupils in the six schools, 360 were offered places by lottery, because tutor capacity was limited; the remaining 120 formed the comparison group. Because places were allocated at random, the comparison is a fair one: the two groups had near-identical prior attainment, attendance and demographic profiles at the start of the year.

Results
Progress was measured using the standardised Year 7 mathematics assessment, taken in September 2024 and again in June 2025.

Group | Pupils assessed in June | Mean score, Sept 2024 | Mean score, June 2025 | Gain
Tutored | 342 | 88.0 | 98.6 | 10.6
Comparison | 114 | 87.8 | 93.4 | 5.6

Tutored pupils gained 10.6 points against 5.6 for the comparison group, a gain 89% larger. The difference of five points is equivalent to roughly four months of additional progress, and is in line with the effects reported in the national evidence base for small-group tutoring. Attendance at sessions averaged 87%, and 95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme.

Teachers in all six schools reported that tutored pupils were more confident in lessons, and four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue.

Proposal
We propose to extend the programme to all eligible Year 7 pupils in the county's 42 secondary schools from September 2026, retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks, delivered in school hours by trained university-student tutors. Riverside University has agreed in principle to expand its recruitment, and its Education Department will continue to train and pay tutors.

Around 3,100 pupils a year meet the eligibility criterion across the 42 schools. Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus; the remaining 16 are in or near Riverside itself, within a short bus ride of the campus, as were all six pilot schools.

Cost
The pilot cost £750 per tutored pupil: £480 in tutor pay (90 hours of tutoring per group, shared among three pupils, at £16 an hour), £220 for university coordination and training, and £50 for materials and assessment. Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million.

This compares favourably with the Authority's current spending on Year 8 and Year 9 catch-up classes, which cost £1,100 per pupil and have shown no measurable effect on attainment in the last two internal evaluations. We propose that the catch-up budget be wound down over two years and the savings redirected to tutoring.

Risks and mitigations
Tutor quality. All tutors will complete the University's 12-hour training course and be observed twice per term by a school mathematics lead.
Timetabling. Sessions will be scheduled during form time and one weekly mathematics lesson, as in the pilot, so pupils do not miss other subjects.
Evaluation. The Policy Unit will continue to track progress using the standardised assessment and will report to Committee annually.

Recommendation
The pilot provides rigorous, randomised evidence that high-dose tutoring substantially accelerates progress for pupils who start secondary school behind in mathematics. The model is proven and its costs are known. We recommend that the Committee approve £2.9 million a year from September 2026 to extend tutoring to all 42 secondary schools, funded in part by winding down the catch-up class budget.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million." -- 3,100 pupils x £750 = £2,325,000 (about £2.3 million), not £2.9 million. The headline cost repeated in the summary and recommendation does not follow from the stated unit cost and pupil numbers.
2. [inconsistency] at: "the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks" -- The pilot is described (and costed) as tutoring in groups of three pupils, but the proposal says it will retain 'the one-to-one format used in the pilot'. The delivery format contradicts itself, and the unit cost depends on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus" -- The scale-up assumes the same university-student tutor model and the same unit cost, yet the document states that 26 of 42 schools are 40-75 miles from the University while all pilot schools were a short bus ride away. Tutor travel time/cost and tutor supply for rural schools are never addressed, though the conclusion ('the model is proven and its costs are known') depends on them.

REVIEW:
# Review: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Maths

The pilot evidence is good, but the brief does not support its conclusion that the model is "proven and its costs are known". The costing is wrong, and the proposal differs materially from what was piloted.

## Major problems

**1. The £2.9m figure doesn't follow from the stated unit cost.**
3,100 × £750 = **£2.325m**, not £2.9m. £2.9m implies about £935 per pupil. Either the arithmetic is wrong or there is an unstated cost assumption (travel, say). The brief should reconcile this before Committee sees it. The author's claim that the annual figure "follows directly" is false.

**2. The proposal changes the format, which breaks the costing.**
The pilot used groups of three. The Proposal section says "the one-to-one format used in the pilot". That is a factual error, and if it reflects real intent it is a major change. The £480 tutor-pay line works only because 90 hours are shared among three pupils. One-to-one would cost £1,440 per pupil in tutor pay, a unit cost of about £1,710 and an annual bill of roughly **£5.3m**. The effect size was also measured only for small-group tutoring. The author's claim of "same format" is contradicted by the document.

**3. The scale-up is not "the same" for 26 of 42 schools.**
All six pilot schools were a short bus ride from the university. Twenty-six of the 42 schools are 40–75 miles away. The brief doesn't address:
- tutor travel time and cost, or whether students will commute that far at £16 an hour
- whether there are enough tutors in rural areas
- observation and quality assurance by school maths leads in those schools
- whether the effect holds in different contexts, since the pilot schools were urban

None of this is in the unit cost, so the real cost is understated further.

**4. Tutor supply and coordination are assumed to scale.**
The pilot needed tutors for 360 pupils, about 120 groups. Full rollout covers about 3,100 pupils, roughly 1,000 groups, so about 8–9 times as many tutors. The pilot used the same training route and the same Education Department, but "agreed in principle" is not a commitment. The coordination cost (£220) is also unlikely to stay flat at nine times the volume, or to hold across 42 schools and long distances. "Same tutors" is impossible at this scale.

**5. The funding offset is weak.**
- Savings from winding down catch-up classes arrive over two years, but the full cost starts in September 2026.
- Catch-up classes serve Years 8 and 9, and tutoring serves Year 7, so the pupils differ. "No measurable effect" in two internal evaluations is not evidence that the budget can be cut without harm, and nothing is said about the quality of those evaluations.
- The brief doesn't say how much is saved or how large the funding gap is.
- The £1,100 comparison is per pupil, but the eligible numbers differ, so it isn't like-for-like.

## Evidence and framing issues

- **Overclaiming.** "Proven", "rigorous" and "sure thing" rest on one pilot, one cohort, six schools and one year. There is no follow-up on whether gains persist. The results table has no confidence intervals or significance test. The "four months of additional progress" conversion is unsourced.
- **Pilot schools weren't randomly chosen.** Randomisation was within schools. The causal estimate is credible for those schools, but it does not extend automatically to rural schools.
- **Soft evidence.** Teacher-reported confidence and four of six head teachers asking to continue are unblinded and anecdotal. The brief doesn't say what the other two wanted.
- **Timetabling.** Using "one weekly mathematics lesson" for sessions means tutored pupils missed regular maths teaching. The claim that pupils "do not miss other subjects" sidesteps this, and it matters for interpreting and replicating the effect.
- **The evaluation plan is weaker than the pilot.** Universal rollout removes the comparison group, so future "tracking" can't show causal impact. A staggered or phased rollout, for example starting with the 16 near-campus schools and randomising the order for the rest, would keep the evidence and reduce risk.
- **Timeline.** The brief is dated January 2026 and proposes a September 2026 start. If that has passed, the dates and the funding profile need updating.

## What holds up

- The pilot arithmetic is internally consistent. The gains are 10.6 and 5.6, the difference is 5.0, which is 89% larger. The 87% attendance and 95% completion figures are consistent with 342/360 and 114/120.
- The £750 breakdown sums correctly (£480 + £220 + £50).
- Lottery allocation and near-identical baselines make the within-pilot comparison credible.

## Recommendation

Don't take this to Committee as written. At minimum:
1. Correct the cost (£2.3m at pilot unit cost, or the true figure).
2. Fix or justify the one-to-one versus group-of-three discrepancy and re-cost.
3. Add rural delivery, travel and tutor-supply costs and plans.
4. Get a firm commitment from the University on tutor numbers.
5. Replace "proven" with language that reflects a single pilot, and consider a phased, evaluable rollout.
